summary: A stack is a linear collection with LIFO (last in, first out) access: only the top is accessible. Push adds to the top, pop removes from it, all in O(1).

sections.heading: Operations
bullets: push(x): add x on top. O(1).
pop(): remove and return the top. O(1).
peek()/top(): read the top without removing. O(1).
Overflow: push onto a full fixed-size stack. Underflow: pop from an empty one.

sections.heading: Array implementation
sections.body: Keep an array and an index `top` (-1 when empty). Push increments top then stores; pop reads then decrements. Fixed capacity unless you grow the array (amortized O(1) push).

sections.heading: Linked-list implementation
sections.body: Push and pop at the head of a singly linked list. No capacity limit, but each element carries a pointer and a malloc.

sections.heading: Applications
bullets: Function calls: the call stack stores frames and return addresses.
Monotonic stack problems (next greater element, largest rectangle).

sections.body: Push each opening bracket; on a closing bracket pop and check that it matches. The string is balanced if every pop matches and the stack ends empty.
Scan tokens: push numbers; on an operator pop two operands, apply, push the result. `3 4 + 2 *` gives 14. Dijkstra's shunting-yard algorithm converts infix to postfix using an operator stack.
Every recursive call pushes a frame. Deep recursion can overflow the stack; any recursion can be converted to iteration with an explicit stack, which is how iterative DFS works.
Keep a stack of indices with decreasing values. When a larger value arrives, pop and resolve each smaller one. Each element is pushed and popped once, so total O(n).

takeaways: LIFO: only the top is accessible; push/pop/peek are O(1).
Implement with an array (fast, bounded) or a linked list (unbounded).
Powers recursion, undo, parsing, and DFS.
